vignette:
Jeremy is thirty years old, a carpenter, and he has been married to his wife, Leah, for six years. He came to see me at his wife’s urging, though he is careful to say it was his own choice. He sits forward in the chair, forearms on his knees, hands clasped. He is broad-shouldered and quiet, and he looks at the floor when he speaks about the thing that happened.

It was a Wednesday in early October, about eight months ago. He was on a job site, a new apartment complex going up on the east side of the city. He was on the third floor, running baseboard with a trim gun. He remembers the smell of fresh sawdust and the low hum of a table saw somewhere below. He heard shouting first—angry, sharp—then the sound of something heavy hitting concrete. He went to the open window and looked down. Two men were fighting in the parking lot below. One of them, a younger guy in a red hoodie, had a knife. Jeremy watched the knife go in. He watched the other man fall. He remembers the way the man’s knees buckled, the way he tried to catch himself on the air. The man in the red hoodie ran. The man on the ground made a sound that Jeremy can still hear, a wet, rattling breath. He was dead by the time the paramedics got there. Jeremy watched them try. He watched them stop.

He did not know the man. He did not know the man who killed him. He gave a statement to the police, then he went home. He thought he was fine. He showered. He ate dinner. He watched a show with Leah. He went to sleep. But the next day, he could not go back to the job site. He told his foreman he had a stomach bug. He stayed home for three days. He could not explain why. He just felt wrong. He felt like his skin was too tight.

Now, eight months later, he has stopped driving past that part of the city. He takes the long way around, even if it adds twenty minutes to his commute. He has stopped working on any job that is above the first floor. He tells his boss he has vertigo. He has started to check the locks on his doors three times before he can fall asleep. He lies in bed and he replays the sound of that wet breath. He sees the man’s hand open and close on the pavement. He feels the weight of the trim gun in his own hand, and he wonders if he could have done something. Should have done something. He did not, of course. He just watched. He stood at the window and watched.

Leah has told him he is not himself. He is short with her. He does not want to go out to dinner or to see her friends. He does not want to be in crowds. He says he is tired, which is true. He is exhausted. He sleeps badly, and when he does sleep, he dreams of the knife going in, over and over, from different angles, as if his brain is trying to find a version where it does not happen. He wakes up sweating, his heart hammering, and he does not tell Leah what he saw. He does not tell anyone. He thinks about it constantly, and he thinks about how he is supposed to be fine. He is a carpenter. He builds things. He is supposed to be steady. He is supposed to be okay. He is not okay. He does not know how to say that.
